title: A pounding headache at C6
objective: Recognize autonomic dysreflexia in injuries at or above T6 (sudden severe hypertension, headache) and look first for a distended bladder or bowel

brief.situation: 14:00 in a neuro ICU. You are Mr. Lewis's nurse. He is 29, on day 12 after a complete C6 spinal cord injury, breathing on his own, waiting for a rehab bed. He calls out: 'My head is pounding.'
handover: His usual blood pressure is about 98/60 with a heart rate in the 60s. He is lying flat after a turn at 13:30.
Indwelling urinary catheter; an abdominal binder and compression stockings. No bowel movement since three days ago.

Unit protocol for autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, loosen anything tight, check blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes, check the catheter and bladder first, then the bowel; the ordered fast-acting antihypertensive if systolic stays over 150; tell the intensivist.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

The authored point of a hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage or seizure. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Sat up within 2 minutes of the blood pressure (protocol: immediately).
The catheter fixed within 10 minutes of the blood pressure (authored target). FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The intensivist told within 5 minutes (unit practice).
Observation with blood pressure every few minutes until it settles: about 25 min.

why.question: What is happening to Mr. Lewis, and what do you look for and do first?

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Autonomic dysreflexia: an injury at or above T6 (C6); systolic 20-40 mmHg or more above baseline with a pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the injury and a slow pulse, from a noxious stimulus below it.
parts.modelAnswer: This is autonomic dysreflexia. With a C6 injury, something below the injury is triggering a huge reflex: his pressure is far above his baseline, his pulse is slow, his head is pounding and he's flushed and sweating above the injury.

parts.label: What first
parts.criteria: Sits him up and loosens tight items at once; checks the bladder and catheter first (kinks, distension) and drains it, then the bowel; blood pressure every 2-5 minutes; antihypertensive only if systolic stays over 150; never lies him flat; tells the intensivist.
parts.modelAnswer: Sit him up and loosen the binder and stockings right away, then find the trigger, bladder first: the catheter is kinked, so straighten it and drain it, then check the bowel. Pressure every few minutes, and the ordered antihypertensive only if it stays over 150. Don't lie him flat. Tell the intensivist.

noProgress.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia untreated for an hour is harm here.

expertPath.text: Blood pressure far above his baseline with a slow pulse: sit him up, legs down.
Loosen the binder and stockings. Check the catheter: kinked, 850 mL in the bladder.
Straighten and drain. Tell the intensivist. Pressure every 2 to 5 minutes.
Document; teach him to report a pounding headache at once.

bleed.headline: Brain hemorrhage
bleed.body: In an injury at or above T6, sudden severe hypertension with a pounding headache is autonomic dysreflexia. Sit up, loosen, and find the trigger, bladder first.

settled.headline: Reversed
settled.body: You recognized autonomic dysreflexia, sat him up at once, found the kinked catheter and drained it, and told the intensivist. That is the expert path.

settledGaps.headline: Settled, with gaps
settledGaps.body: Check how fast you sat him up and found the bladder, and whether he was laid flat or given acetaminophen instead.

time_up.headline: Unresolved
time_up.body: Autonomic dysreflexia needs the trigger found within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Mr. Lewis has a C6 injury, above T6. A pressure far above his baseline of about 98/60, a slow pulse, a pounding headache, and flushing and sweating above the injury is autonomic dysreflexia: a noxious stimulus below the injury drives a reflex his brain cannot dampen. Sit him up and lower his legs at once, loosen the binder and stockings, and check the pressure every 2 to 5 minutes. Look for the trigger, bladder first: the catheter is kinked and the bladder holds 850 mL, so straighten and drain it; then check the bowel. Use the ordered antihypertensive only if systolic stays over 150 after that. Never lie him flat, and don't treat the headache as simple pain.
